reference.source: ICHD-3 / International Classification of Sleep Disorders
clinicalPearls: Recurrent episodes of inability to move the trunk and limbs while falling asleep or on waking, with full awareness of the surroundings
Episodes last seconds to a few minutes and resolve spontaneously or when the person is touched or spoken to
Frightening hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations are common, such as a sensed intruder, chest pressure or a floating sensation
The term isolated indicates that it occurs without narcolepsy, and recurrent troublesome episodes define the disorder
It represents intrusion of the muscle atonia of REM sleep into wakefulness
Sleep deprivation, irregular sleep schedules, the supine position and psychological stress are recognised precipitants
Management centres on reassurance and improved sleep habits, while persistent daytime sleepiness or cataplexy should prompt evaluation for narcolepsy
reference.pathophysiology: Sleep paralysis occurs when the muscle atonia that normally accompanies REM sleep persists into, or intrudes upon, wakefulness at the boundaries of sleep. The person is conscious but temporarily unable to move voluntary muscles, while dream-related imagery may carry over as vivid hallucinations. Factors that disrupt or fragment REM sleep, such as sleep deprivation and irregular schedules, increase the likelihood of these dissociated states.
additionalDifferentials: Narcolepsy, in which sleep paralysis is one feature
Nocturnal seizures, for example of frontal lobe origin
additionalInvestigations: Clinical history establishing the timing, preserved awareness and brief duration of episodes
Screening for narcolepsy features such as excessive sleepiness and cataplexy
Sleep diary and assessment of sleep deprivation and schedule regularity
Polysomnography and multiple sleep latency testing if narcolepsy is suspected
Review of stress, psychiatric symptoms and substance use
redFlags: Excessive daytime sleepiness or cataplexy suggesting narcolepsy
Features atypical for sleep paralysis that suggest nocturnal seizures
Episodes occurring away from the sleep-wake transition
Severe distress or avoidance of sleep because of the episodes
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and often improves with better sleep habits and reassurance; episodes may recur intermittently, especially with sleep loss or stress, but do not indicate serious disease once narcolepsy has been excluded.
pitfalls: Missing underlying narcolepsy when sleepiness or cataplexy is also present
Mistaking episodes for nocturnal seizures or panic attacks
Underestimating the fear and sleep avoidance the episodes can cause
Neglecting sleep deprivation and irregular schedules as remediable triggers
references: International Classification of Sleep Disorders, 3rd edition (ICSD-3)
Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine (Kryger, Roth, Dement)
management: Reassure and explain that episodes are benign intrusions of REM-sleep atonia into wakefulness once narcolepsy is excluded
Reinforce sleep hygiene with regular schedules and adequate sleep duration to reduce REM fragmentation
Address precipitants by avoiding sleep deprivation, discouraging the supine sleeping position and managing psychological stress
Treat comorbid anxiety, depression or stress that provoke episodes
Consider REM-suppressing antidepressant therapy only for frequent, distressing episodes
Screen for narcolepsy features such as excessive sleepiness and cataplexy, and refer to sleep medicine for polysomnography if an underlying disorder is suspected
